en: Her frenzy subsided,
Her mind cleared in contemplation,
The grime upon her heart fell away,
And strength entered and filled her.
Overcome with joy, she trembled:
“I have repented ninetyfold,” she said,
Bowing her dear head down to the earth.
“Uncle Joltay, may you live long;
I have always looked to you for shelter.
I will not assail you with harsh words;
You are the spiritual guide I humbly implore,
And I will never cease to hope in you.”
Thus spoke Akbermet.
As she stood there in this wondrous state,
And finished speaking
To her uncle Joltay, the gray wolf,
Seytek readied himself like a hawk;
Into the lion Seytek’s mind
An inspiration came from the unseen.
In a dream, his forefather hero Manas
Revealed an auspicious vision.
It was his forefather Manas himself,
The radiant one supporting and sustaining him,
Who had come to visit him then.
He placed a sword in my hand,
And spoke at length of its thousand-fold lineage:
“Take heed, my child,” he said,
“You are my joy, you are my root,
You are the heir who carries on my legacy.
In this worthless, deceitful world,
Do not be vainly tempted, my child;
Do not chill the people’s hearts.
Do not lord it over those beneath you,
And never treat the poor, the orphaned, the wretched
With contempt, my son!
My forefather Manas said these words:
‘Here is Zulpuqor before you;
I give it to you, my son—take it.
A son as keen as Zulpuqor
Will come into your arms.
When you take this sword in hand,
Whoever faces you will swiftly perish;
When you strike straight, it will blaze like fire.
The land you charge against will be laid waste,
And its people will despair of life.
Of every hostile enemy,
It will level the innermost fortress.
When you draw it, its edge will glow red.
I give it to you, my son—take it,
Bind it firmly to your arm,
Do not loose it toward whatever lies before you,
But guard it securely and wait.
Solitude is suffering,’ he said.
‘All the cares that weigh upon your life—
May you sweep every one of them away.
God willing, a son will be born;
Name him Kenen.
If that son survives,
My child, he himself will inherit from you.
That son will be of the ancient line,
A lofty plane tree, a proud banner to his foes,
With eyes like deep and boundless springs,
The very image of a gray-maned wolf.
Prize the sword and place it in its sheath;
Then go against the enemy
Who flaunts his might and boasts,
Spill his blood and turn him back.
If a hostile foe advances upon you,
Break his back when you meet,
Still his heart when you clash,
Spilling blood and scorching the earth.
Wage the struggle fiercely!’
Thus spoke my grandfather,
And when he spread his hands and said, ‘Amen,’
There were eighty men behind him
And eight men before him.
When my forefather gave his blessing,
They all gave their blessing too.
Their white beards gleamed like pale silk,
Their shining teeth were like copper,
Their blue eyes were round as great bowls,
Their splendor seemed enough to swallow one’s soul.
All were gathered there together:
Almambet and Chubak among them,
And the elders Koshoy and Bakai.
With a great roar they raised their hands—
All the companions
Of my lion-hearted father Manas.
Having received the heroes’ blessing,
I awoke with a start from sleep.
It was a dream seen by grace,
With my forefather Manas at their head;
It was a day when blessings were bestowed,
A wondrous and auspicious thing,
A dream from which I woke in alarm.
What might this dream of mine portend?
Let uncle Akjoltoy interpret it now!”
Then his uncle Joltay
Readied himself like a hawk,
And prayed to the spirit
Of the hero who had passed into the next world:
“May your dream, my child, come true.
If your forefather gave you Zulpuqor,
Then the sovereign God Himself
Has surely granted you a child.
A hero full-grown—a son—
Oh, my dear, He has clearly granted you one.
That Koshoy gave his blessing
Means he blessed the child as well.
Dark gray, a hero in his purest form,
Dark-flanked and blue-gray without,
He will have a noble bearing,
And a mane flowing down his back.
His hand will be fierce and open against the foe,
And when he sets out, his road will lie open.
He will subdue whoever he confronts;
His valor will be beyond compare,
A peerless champion, a foremost eagle.
You will have a gray-wolf son,
And you will name him Kenen.
That son whom you saw
Will become an unwavering banner;
Wherever his desire turns, an uproar will rise.
Those who heed his words
He will master through speech,
While fools who will not understand
He will scatter in direct slaughter.
He will make the witless plead for mercy
And subdue the hot-tempered.
His surge will be like a lake’s swift current,
His courage like a blazing flame.
You are destined to have a son.
May this dream of ours come true,
May true sacred power prevail,
May fortune and abundance come in full.
May blessings come to the teeming people,
Inexhaustible however freely they partake.
May God grant him land on which to live,
And, so that he may sustain the people,
May He grant a tiger-limbed hero
Whose keenness is like Zulpuqor’s.
May every word he speaks be fitting;
Trusting in the Creator’s protection,
May Kenen’s cradle-cord be firm!”
Thus Akjoltoy spoke,
Interpreting the dream with precision,
Explaining it fully without tiring,
Unfolding meanings of many kinds,
Interpreting it with surpassing accuracy,
And so he finished reading the dream.
“Here are sixty head, beginning with horses,
For my uncle Joltay,” he said,
And gave them as his interpreter’s reward.
He gave double-humped camels,
And livestock of all four kinds,
Red gold and ornaments,
Yellow-mottled cloth with a silken weave,
Heavy black-mottled fabric,
Bales of goods bound for transport,
And red-gold coins.
He took a red camel won as booty,
And an elephant fit for bearing loads.
Joltay’s heart was content;
He became immeasurably rich,
His hollows filled with milk,
His wants filled with meat.
Joyful and at ease,
Through all of this Akjoltoy
Became a wealthy man tending countless herds.
KENEN
THE BIRTH OF KENEN
The moon waned and days passed,
Many more days passed,
Nine months were fulfilled,
And after nine more days had passed,
When her time was complete,
The unfortunate noblewoman
Went into labor.
Her waist ached above,
Where death might strike, it ached,
Both her dark thighs ached,
Every bone, limb, and sinew,
Without exception, ached,
Her frail soul screamed,
Unable to endure, she sobbed,
Her ribs seemed torn apart,
As though it would take her life now,
The poor lady was utterly spent,
As though bowing low, she would surrender her life,
So grievous were her labor pains,
Her life hung by a single hair,
Her thoughts scattered in a thousand directions,
Her frail soul was blown away,
She strained and writhed,
Her bewildered mind was divided,
That accursed, merciless death
Now appeared before her eyes,
Worn down by torment,
Seeing no hope, she despaired of life,
When the fiercest labor came,
For life is sweet until death,
She kept writhing in agony.
At midnight,
When her labor came to term,
When the appointed hour was fulfilled,
Sixty old matrons
Waited in a circle around her,
What a wondrous sight it was,
A figure blessed with sacred grace,
The wonder of it was this:
The moon rose upon his brow,
The sun stood above his crown,
His perfect fortune set forth,
The fierce black-maned leopard—
She gave birth to brave Kenen.
The child dropped forth crying,
Shouting every battle cry,
He landed upright on his soles,
His kin rejoiced,
But the hateful enemy who begrudged him
Felt his breast split apart.
He bore every heroic sign,
And when they looked at his back,
He had a black mane a span long,
All the old women scurried,
And all the young wives,
Saying, “What an extraordinary horror!
This is no child but a calamity,
He is something wholly different,
He has a roaring voice,
Hair grows upon his back,
Fur covers his body,
He is one who will leave none unharmed,
The black eye of disaster!”
Losing their senses,
As though he might seize and swallow a young child,
They panicked and trembled,
Many fled in terror,
Many muttered incantations,
And many among the people grumbled.
The noble Gulayym,
The true lady, peer of princes,
The capable lady in all she did,
Purest among those with brass thimbles,
Foremost among the scarf-wearing women,
Said to the old women who were fleeing,
“Fall down and be damned,
May grave dust fill your eyes!”
She scattered earth and chanted,
Performing many different rites,
Invoking Baabedin’s blessing,
Naming a horse for the crescent hoof,
Then slowly turned,
And before the child upon the shield,
The luckless woman repented,
Bowing as young wives do,
